A LITTLE CONTEXT

Get to know the table.

Numbers tell a story

Atomic number counts protons. A neutral atom has the same number of electrons. The chemical symbol is an element’s short name; the period is its horizontal row.

Families share patterns

Colors identify element categories. Groups are vertical columns. Lanthanides and actinides belong to periods 6 and 7; they sit below to keep the table compact.

Electrons shape chemistry

Valence electrons help atoms bond. Main-group counts use the outer shell; transition-metal counts include s and d electrons. Inner-transition elements need extra care.

Scientific notes & sources

Atomic masses use the CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights, including the 2024 revisions, with uncertainties shown in each detail panel. These are averages for normal terrestrial materials; individual isotopes have different masses. Standard atomic weight is dimensionless; its numerical value gives the corresponding average atomic mass in u.

Bracketed integers come from the IUPAC May 2022 periodic table. They identify the mass number (protons + neutrons) of the isotope with the longest confirmed half-life in that edition, not a standard atomic weight or exact isotope mass.

Valence conventions follow OpenStax’s electron-configuration discussion. For d-block elements we show the formal s + d count; it is not a bond count or oxidation state. For lanthanides and actinides we show the outermost-shell count; f and d electrons can also participate in bonding. Lawrencium uses the 7s²7p¹ ground-state assignment.

Categories are an educational convention: group 12 is included with the transition metals, polonium with post-transition metals, and astatine with halogens. Superheavy-element categories and main-group valence counts follow table position; their chemistry is not fully established. See the Royal Society of Chemistry for individual element references.
